newsitem.title: ANGOLA: First private investment bank launched in Angola.
newsitem.headline: First private investment bank launched in Angola.

text.p: Angola's state-owned oil company Sonangol and 26 private shareholders mainly from Europe, South Africa and the United States have together set up Angola's first private investment bank.
The new Banco Africano de Investimentos (BAI), with a capital base of $32.5 million rand, was officially inaugurated on Thursday by Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
Angolan shareholders have a 37.5 percent share in the bank while Sonangol is the major player with 17.5 percent.
State diamond company Endiama holds 1.5 percent and businessman and head of Angola's TecnoCarro compan, Jose Recio has a seven percent share in the bank.
Portuguese shareholders with a total 33 percent share in BAI include Caixa Central de Credito Agricola, Banco de Investimento and Banco Pinto & Sotto Mayor, Soares da Costa and the Mota group.
Other foreign companies, making up 29.5 percent of the bank, include South Africa's Investec Bank Ltd, with 7.5 percent.
France's Brenco trading company and Florida-based Amercon International each have a six percent stake.

BAI president, former Angolan finance minister and African Development Bank member in Abidjan, Aguinaldo Jaime, told Reuters the bank wanted to help Angola relaunch its economy which was devastated by civil war.
Fighting between the government and former rebel UNITA movement ended in 1994 with the signing of the Lusaka Protocol.
"We believe we have a very important role to play in mobilising external and domestic savings in order to finance projects and programmes to modernise Angola's economy," Jaime said.
He said the bank wanted to bring on board reliable foreign partners to supplement the lack of internal savings in Angola.

"Domestic savings is not enough. One of the weaknesses of the African economy is the low rate of internal savings which is why...we had to attract foreign and reliable partners to supplement the internal savings," he said.
Jaime said shareholders believed the Angolan government was serious about economic reform and that peace would hold.
"We think the government is embarking on a programme of economic reform and part of this is the liberalisation of the financial system," he said.
While the focus on the bank would be on investment, it would also look at commercial activities.
"Our main focus will be investment activities, but we will be looking at some commercial activities as well," Jaime said.
The bank's first branch abroad would probably be opened in Lisbon, Portugal next month.
